Research article
Integrated aerobic-anaerobic digestion of highly solids-loaded corn stover
and swine manure under dynamic aeration: Temperature rise,
physicochemical characteristics, and methane production
Lili Wang 1, Zicong Wang 1, Zhongjiang Wang *, Jingke Zheng
College of Engineering, Northeast Agricultural University, Harbin, 150030, China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Integrated aerobic-anaerobic digestion
Aerobic pretreatment
Dynamic aeration
Corn stover
Swine manure
Methane production
A B S T R A C T
This research aimed to design an integrated aerobic-anaerobic reactor with dynamic aeration that was auto-
matically regulated based on real-time oxygen concentration and investigate the aerobic pretreatment and
subsequent dry co-anaerobic digestion (co-AD) characteristics of highly solids-loaded corn stover and swine
manure in terms of temperature rise, physiochemical characteristics, and methane production. The high-
temperature feedstocks from the aerobic pretreatment phase rapidly entered the AD phase without trans-
portation and effectively improved the start-up and methane production of the co-AD. Oxygen concentration
range, aeration rate, and pretreatment time affected the cumulative aeration time, temperature rise, and organic
matter removal interactively during aerobic pretreatment, and a low aeration rate was relatively preferable.
Although the lignocellulose removal increased with the increase in pretreatment duration, the maximal lignin
elimination efficiency only reached 1.30%. The inoculum injection in the transition phase from aerobic pre-
treatment to co-AD and the leachate reflux during co-AD were also critical for producing methane steadily apart
from aerobic pretreatment. The cold air weakened the temperature rise of aerobic pretreatment, and the low-
temperature leachate reduced the methane production in the co-AD process. An oxygen concentration range
of 13%–17%, aeration rate of 0.10 m3/(min⋅m3), pretreatment time of 84 h, inoculum loading of 40%, leachate
refluxing thrice per day, and double-layer inoculation were optimum for improving the integrated aerobic-
anaerobic digestion system’s ability to resist low temperatures and achieving high methane production. The
maximal cumulative and volatile solids (VS) methane yields of corn stover and swine manure reached 444.58 L
and 266.30 L/kg VS.
1. Introduction
As a primary grain-producing and livestock husbandry country, the
annual outputs of lignocellulosic biomass and livestock manure reach
over 0.7 and 3.05 billion tons in China, with corn stover and swine
manure representing about a third of each (Dong et al., 2023; Zhang
et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024). Generally, feces and wastewater are
collected separately in most Chinese swine breeding farms to save water
resources and reduce wastewater production. Therefore, dry anaerobic
digestion (AD) featuring high solids loading (generally 15%–35%, w/w),
low reactor scale cost, and high methane productivity (Karrabi et al.,
2023) is an environmentally friendly approach for treating corn stover
and swine manure, as well as high-carbon corn stover and high-nitrogen
swine manure can balance the carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratio during
their co-AD and swine manure itself contains lots of microflora that can
quickly adapt to the anaerobic environment and generate methane
(Arias et al., 2020). However, dry AD without pretreatment is prone to
acid and ammonia inhibition due to the compact lignocellulosic struc-
ture of corn stover and the high presence of ammonium in swine manure
(Song et al., 2023).
Aerobic pretreatment mainly includes aerobic or microaerobic hy-
drolysis pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass under low total solids
(TS) loading (≤10%, w/w) (Chu et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2016), air
stripping aiming at reducing ammonium levels of swine wastewater,
digestate et al. before or after anaerobic digestion (Folino et al., 2020),
and aerobic composting of mixed organic feedstocks containing

lignocellulosic biomass, livestock manure et al. under high TS loading
(commonly 30%–50%, w/w) (Guo et al., 2012; Labatut et al., 2011).
Aerobic pretreatment under high solids loading could facilitate an in-
tegrated operation of aerobic and dry-anaerobic equipment, where both
aerobic and anaerobic processes could be in a single reactor instead of
the traditional transportation of pretreated feedstocks from the pre-
treatment reactor to the anaerobic reactor. Multiple reactors could be
operated independently in parallel to match the volume of waste treated
at different scales of small, medium, and large, thereby avoiding heat
and power losses during feedstock transportation, increasing the flexi-
bility of equipment operation, and reducing the running cost. Mean-
while, aerobic pretreatment can break down the lignocellulosic
structure of straw to a certain extent and reduce the ammonium content
of feedstocks, which is favorable for following dry AD. Several docu-
ments expounded that aerobic pretreatment under high solids loading
was conducive to methane production from municipal solid waste and
food waste. For example, Fdez-Güelfo et al. (2011) pretreated municipal
solid waste and increased the methane yield by 73%. Angeriz-Campoy
et al. (2023) found that aerobic pretreatment effectively improved the
hydrolysis and acid production stages during the co-AD of municipal
solid waste and food waste. Ali et al. (2018) reported that aerobic pre-
treatment before an anaerobic landfill of municipal solid waste could
effectively reduce the lag phase of methane production. However, the
aerobic pretreatment and subsequent dry co-AD characteristics of
lignocellulosic biomass and livestock manure under high solids loading,
especially the integrated operation of aerobic-anaerobic digestion in the
same reactor, remain unclear.
In addition, aerobic pretreatment under high solids loading can
accumulate a large amount of heat and increase the temperature of
feedstocks due to the metabolic reproduction of thermophilic microor-
ganisms, saving power consumption for heating. Meanwhile, some
facultative hydrolysis and acid-producing bacteria favorable for AD can
enrich during aerobic pretreatment (Lin et al., 2018). However, too
much pretreatment time or excessive ventilation can cause undue loss of
energy and organic matter, and too little treatment time or deficient
ventilation can weaken the pretreatment effect. Dynamic aeration,
which relies on real-time oxygen concentration to control aeration, is
mainly employed in wastewater treatment (Herrmann-Heber et al.,
2020). For aerobic composting, most of the attention focuses on moni-
toring the oxygen concentrations in the exhaust gas at different stages of
the composting process to study the relationship between microbial
activity and oxygen concentrations (Nie, 2000; Puyuelo et al., 2010). It
would not only provide a more suitable oxygen amount to ensure the
metabolism and reproduction of microorganisms, accelerate warming,
and improve pretreatment efficiency but also further reduce energy
consumption and heat loss compared to traditional aeration if dynamic
aeration is employed in the aerobic pretreatment procedure (Zeng et al.,
2022). Therefore, dynamic aeration is promising for enhancing aerobic

addition,
methanogens-enriched inoculum can accelerate the start of AD, avoid
rancidity, and increase the decomposition rate of feedstocks. However,
too much inoculum would affect the efficiency of volumetric methane
production and even inhibit the AD process. The appropriate amount of
inoculum also varies greatly depending on the feedstocks, moisture
content, C/N ratio, and so on (Axelle et al., 2016). The leachate reflux
can reduce the accumulation of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and ammonia
during dry AD due to the mixing difficulty under high solids loading and
improve mass and heat transfer efficiencies. However, excessive flushing
of leachate would destabilize the microbial communities, affecting
methane production (Song et al., 2023). Accordingly, the inoculum in-
jection after aerobic pretreatment and before dry co-AD of corn stover
and swine manure and the leachate reflux during their co-AD are also
critical to ensure stable operation of the integrated aerobic-anaerobic
process. Therefore, exploring the aerobic pretreatment characteristics
and control parameters of corn stover and swine manure with high solids
loading under dynamic aeration and the methanogenic properties of
subsequent dry co-AD are valuable.
This study aims to design a set of aerobic-anaerobic integrated de-
vices with a dynamic aeration system automatically regulated based on
the oxygen concentrations and to investigate the feasibility of fulfilling
the aerobic and dry anaerobic processes in a single reactor. First, the
aerobic pretreatment and subsequent co-AD characteristics of corn sto-
ver and swine manure with high solids loading under dynamic aeration
were studied systematically in terms of temperature rise, physico-
chemical characteristics, and methane production. Second, the effects of
the inoculum addition between aerobic pretreatment and dry co-AD and
the leachate reflux in the dry co-AD phase on methane production were
investigated to realize the rapidly non-intermittent conversion from
aerobic pretreatment to dry co-AD and the stable operation of the dry co-
AD process. The information obtained will help to fill the gaps in the
literature on aerobic pretreatment and methane production from highly
solids-loaded complex biomass and accelerate the widespread applica-
tion of dynamic aeration and scale development of integrated aerobic-
anaerobic digestion.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Feedstocks and inoculum
Air-dried corn stover taken from the corn field of Northeast Agri-
cultural University in China was crushed into 3–5 mm particle size by a
pulverizer (TQ-2500Y, Yongkang Tianqishengshi Instrument Co., Ltd.,
Zhejiang, China) and stored at 20 ± 1.5 ◦C before use. The TS, VS, total
carbon (TC), total nitrogen (TN), cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin
contents of corn stover were 91.85 ± 0.53%, 84.61 ± 0.41%, 44.18 ±0
.018%, 0.68 ± 0.02%, 39.35 ± 0.35%, 29.21 ± 0.28% and 12.04 ±
0.18%, respectively. Swine manure collected from the Guangming
Village breeding base in China was kept at −20 ◦C until use. The inoc-
ulum for co-AD was the biogas slurry of swine manure digested in the
laboratory. The swine manure was anaerobically digested in a 10 L jar at
35 ◦C until the methane production stopped to obtain digestate. The
slurry obtained after removing solids from the digestate was used as
inoculum to avoid clogging in the inoculum addition process. The TS,
VS, TC, TN, cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin contents and the pH
value of swine manure were 27.83 ± 0.65%, 20.41 ± 0.28%, 25.34 ±
0.49%, 1.86 ± 0.13%, 18.17 ± 0.16%, 21.51 ± 0.32%, 7.24 ± 0.39%,
and 6.79 ± 0.41, respectively. The TS, VS, and TN contents and the pH
value of inoculum were 3.28 ± 0.07%, 1.34 ± 0.11%, 5.89 ± 0.26%,
and 7.23 ± 0.03, respectively.
2.2. Aerobic-anaerobic integrated devices with dynamic aeration system
An integrated aerobic-anaerobic reactor is a self-designed cylindrical
polypropylene barrel with a total volume of 80 L, an upper inner
diameter of 550 mm, a lower inner diameter of 400 mm, a height of 750
mm, and a thickness of 2.5 mm, as shown in Fig. 1. The entire outer wall
of the reactor is insulated using a polyurethane blanket with a thickness
of 20 mm (part 10 in Fig. 1). A porous baffle (part 11 in Fig. 1) with a
diameter of 450 mm (aperture of 5 mm) was placed on a support frame
of the reactor bottom to hold the feedstocks and separate the leachate
generated during aerobic pretreatment and co-AD. The aeration holes of
10 mm diameter opened on the upper cover and bottom of the reactor,
respectively, could ensure that the air through the airflow meter and air
blower (parts 2 and 3 in Fig. 1) was injected from the bottom vent and
discharged from the upper vent after forced aeration. Three inlets evenly
opened on the side wall of the reactor realized inoculum injection at the
upper, middle, and lower layer positions on the central axis of the
reactor. Four temperature measurement points set at the upper, middle,
lower, and flank positions inside the reactor corresponded to 450–530,
300–380, and 150–230 mm from the bottom of the reactor, and 75–80
mm from the side wall (TEMupper, TEMmiddle, TEMlower, and TEMflank),
respectively. An electrochemical zirconia sensor probe (part 5 in Fig. 1)

2.3. Aerobic pretreatment and dry anaerobic digestion
The respective additional amount of corn stover and swine manure
directly determine the C/N ratio of mixed feedstocks, and the C/N ratio
and ventilation conditions affect the warming in the aerobic pretreat-
ment process (Kong et al., 2024), which in turn influence the subsequent
co-AD. Furthermore, the threshold values of the oxygen concentration
range and the aeration rate for dynamic aeration were crucial and could
interactively affect the pretreatment effect with the pretreatment
duration. Nie (2000) and Puyuelo et al. (2010) proposed that the mi-
croorganisms were active under oxygen concentrations of 14%–17% and
15%–20% during aerobic composting, respectively. Huang et al. (2019)
reported that the metabolic activities of aerobic microorganisms almost
stopped when the oxygen concentration was less than 10%. The closer
the set upper threshold is to the oxygen concentration of 21% in the
ambient air, the longer the aeration process might run, and the closer the
set lower threshold is to 10%, the more likely the microorganisms might
be in anaerobic conditions (Wang et al., 2024). In addition, Wang et al.
(2022b)Wang et al., 2022a,b, achieved an optimal ventilation rate of
0.20 m3/(min⋅m3) for aerobic composting, while Xu et al. (2018) rec-
ommended a range of ventilation rate [0.05–0.20 m3/(min⋅m3)] for
composting. Therefore, this study first explored the critical control pa-
rameters and pretreatment characteristics of the aerobic process and
then studied the main factors for the rapid start and stable run of the dry
co-AD, namely (1) Aerobic pretreatment experiment I: the effects of the
initial C/N ratios of feedstocks on the temperature rise and lignin
removal during aerobic pretreatment were first studied. The routinely
suitable C/N ratios for aerobic composting and dry AD are 25–35 and
20–30, respectively, with a higher C/N ratio commonly favoring the
warming of feedstocks (Kong et al., 2024). Therefore, three C/N ratios of
25, 30, and 35 (CN1, CN2, and CN3) corresponding to the mass ratios of
corn stover to swine manure of 0.8, 1.3, and 2 (w/w) and three aeration
rates of 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20 m3/(min⋅m3) (R1, R2, and R3) were studied.
The oxygen concentration range, aerobic pretreatment duration, initial
moisture content (MC), and mean room temperature were 13%–17%,
120 h, 60%, and 19.3 ± 2.4 ◦C, respectively. (2) Aerobic pretreatment
experiment II: the temperature rise and physicochemical characteristics
of corn stover and swine manure during aerobic pretreatment under
dynamic aeration were studied systematically. Three oxygen concen-
tration ranges of 9%–13%, 13%–17%, and 17–20% (Aer1, Aer2, and
Aer3), three aeration rates of 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20 m3/(min⋅m3) (R1, R2,
and R3), and three aerobic pretreatment durations of 48, 84, and 120 h
(T1, T2, and T3) were investigated based on three-factor and three-level
orthogonal experiment [L9(33)], as shown in Table 1. The initial MC and
mean room temperature were 60% and 20.4 ± 2.1 ◦C, respectively. (3)
Dry co-AD experiment III: The effects of the aerobic pretreatment under
dynamic aeration on the co-AD characteristics of corn stover and swine
manure were studied. Specifically, the pretreated corn stover and swine
manure after a set pretreatment time was inoculated with an inoculum
loading of 30% (w/w, dry basis) and injected into the two positions of
upper and middle layers, adjusted to a TS content of 20% with tap water,
and then turned off the ventilation system and started the co-AD process.
The constant temperature and duration of co-AD were 35 ◦C and 25
days, respectively. The leachate collected from the bottom of the co-AD
reactor was backflowed twice daily. The corn stover and swine manure
without aerobic pretreatment were a control. (4) Dry co-AD experiment
IV: based on the optimum pretreated results from (1) to (3), the pre-
treatment time (A1: 72 h, A2: 84 h, A3: 96 h), inoculum loading (B1: 20%,
B2: 30%, B3: 40%; w/w, dry basis), leachate reflux repetitions per day
(C1: Once, C2: Twice, C3: Thrice), and the number of inoculum layers
(D1: single-layer, D2: double-layer, and D3: triple-layer corresponding to
the injection postions of the upper layer, upper-middle layers, and
upper-middle-lower layers) on the methanogenic characteristics of
pretreated corn stover and swine manure were further studied. The
mean room temperatures were 18.3 ± 1.7, 17.5 ± 2.3, 17.3 ± 2.4, and

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Temperature rise and lignin removal characteristics of corn stover
and swine manure during aerobic pretreatment under different carbon-to-
nitrogen ratios and aeration rates
As shown in Fig. 2 (a), the temperatures under different C/N ratios
and aeration rates showed a rapid increase followed by a slight decrease.
The upper-layer and middle-layer temperatures were holistically higher
than the lower-layer temperatures, and the flank temperatures were
similar to the middle-layer temperatures. The lower-layer feedstocks
first contacted the incoming air, resulting in more heat dissipation than
other layers (Li et al., 2023). Meanwhile, the leachate gradually seeped
from the upper-layer and middle-layer feedstocks and gathered into the
lower-layer feedstocks, inhibiting the microorganisms because of poor
permeability and oxygen diffusion (Guo et al., 2012). Therefore, the
lower-layer temperature was the lowest compared to other layers.
Moreover, the temperatures under CN3 in the first 48 h were slightly
higher than those under CN1 and CN2, while the temperatures under CN2
from 72 h were higher than those under CN1 and CN3. All the
upper-layer temperatures under CN3 exceeded 60 ◦C at 48 h and reached
the maximal 62.2, 60.9, and 61.1 ◦C under R1, R2, and R3, respectively.
Under CN2, the maximal temperatures under R1, R2, and R3 were ob-
tained at upper-layer, middle-layer, and upper-layer positions, respec-
tively, and reached 62.5, 61.9, and 61.5 ◦C at 72 h. For CN1, only the
upper-layer temperature under CN1R1 reached 60.3 ◦C at 96 h. There-
fore, a high C/N ratio of 35 contributed to warming the feedstocks in the
first 48 h. However, the aerobic pretreatment under a moderate C/N
ratio of 30 also showed a favorable warming trend during the 120-h
treatment.
In addition, C is the energy source for microorganisms, while N is the
nutrient consumed for cell proliferation. Microorganisms assimilate
approximately one part of N for every five parts of C to form cell bodies.
Meanwhile, microorganisms generally consume twenty parts of organic
C to obtain energy when they assimilate and utilize five parts of C.
Consequently, the C/N ratios were decreased after aerobic pretreatment,
as shown in Fig. 2 (b). The final C/N ratios under R1, R2, and R3
decreased to 21.16, 22.04, and 20.51 for CN1, 25.33, 26.40, and 25.94
for CN2, and 29.70, 30.24, and 30.87 for CN3, respectively. Therefore,
the final C/N ratios of the aerobic-pretreated feedstocks were directly
suitable for the following co-AD. In addition, the microorganisms
degrading lignocellulose are mainly the actinomycetes and fungi that
prefer high temperatures (Lin et al., 2018). However, the lignin re-
movals under different C/N ratios and aeration rates only reached
0.87%–1.18%, and CN2R3 was optimum. Therefore, the lignin in the
corn stover could not be well removed during the aerobic pretreatment
with high solids loading and short duration, which was consistent with
the general results of aerobic pretreatment at high solids loading (Wu
et al., 2022). Considering the characteristics of temperature rise and
lignin removal, a C/N ratio of 30 was favorable.
3.2. Effects of oxygen concentration, aeration rate, and time on the
temperature rise and physicochemical properties of corn stover and swine
manure during aerobic pretreatment
3.2.1. Temperature rise and moisture content
As shown in Fig. 3 (a), the temperatures rapidly increased and then
slightly decreased, following similar fluctuations as in Fig. 2 (a). The
upper-layer and middle-layer temperatures were holistically higher than
the lower-layer temperatures, and the flank temperatures were close to
the middle-layer temperatures. The heating rates under Aer1 and Aer2
oxygen concentrations were relatively faster than Aer3, and the optimal
temperature rise occurred under Aer2. The maximal temperatures of
Aer2R2T3 at four temperature measuring points exceeded 60 ◦C at
72–96 h. Only the upper-layer and middle-layer temperatures out-
stripped 60 ◦C for Aer2R1T2 at 72–84 h, whereas its upper, middle, and
flank measurement points simultaneously reached their maximal tem-
peratures at 72 h. The temperature of 65.6 ◦C obtained at the upper-
layer position of Aer2R1T2 when 72 h was the highest during the aero-
bic pretreatment in this study. Therefore, the oxygen concentration and
aeration rate interactively affected the temperature rise, and excessive
aeration was not conducive to heating up. Aer2, R1, and R2 were
favorable for the temperature rise of aerobic pretreatment. In addition,
the initial C/N ratio and oxygen concentration range under CN2 and
Aer2 were identical, whereas the ambient temperatures under CN2
showed a decreased tendency after 24 h, which was subject to overcast
skies, rain, cold fronts, and other stochastic weather influences. In
comparison, the ambient temperatures under Aer2 tended to be warmer
from 24 to 72 h, followed by a decrease after 72 h, but still were higher
than those under CN2. Consequently, the temperatures at different
temperature measurement points obtained under CN2 after 24 h were
lower than those obtained under Aer2, and the maximal temperature
(62.5 ◦C) obtained under CN2R1 was also inferior to that (65.6 ◦C) ob-
tained under Aer2R1T2 (Figs. 2–3), which indicated that the shock of
cold air diminished the activity of microorganisms and weakened the
temperature-rise effectiveness of aerobic pretreatment because the
aerobic pretreatment experiments were using unheated ambient air for
aeration at room temperature.
The heat released during microorganisms breaking down organic
matter could evaporate moisture apart from heating the feedstocks.
Meanwhile, the leachate continually outflew from the bottom of the
reactor. Therefore, an entire downward trend was in MC except
Aer1R1T1, Aer1R2T2, Aer1R3T3, Aer2R2T3, and Aer3R1T3 showed a slight
upward trend in the first 24 h, as shown in Fig. 3 (b). A possible reason
for the increased phenomenon is that the moisture generated by mi-
crobial degradation of organic matter was more than that lost during
ventilation in the early stages of aerobic treatment (Chowdhury et al.,
2014). The MCs under Aer3 decreased the fastest apart from Aer3R1T3,
followed by Aer2, and the moisture lost the slowest under Aer1. There-
fore, the higher the oxygen concentration, the greater the moisture loss.
The oxygen concentrations of 17%–20% under Aer3 were closer to the
oxygen concentration of about 21% in the ambient air, and the aeration
started as soon as the oxygen concentration dropped to below 17%. The
microorganisms could obtain sufficient oxygen, whereas moisture and
heat were more lost because the convective latent heat and moisture
losses carried away by air flowing through the feedstocks were the main
heat losses during ventilation (Ajmal et al., 2020), which was also the
key reason for the relatively low temperatures under Aer3. Although the
microbial activity and heat production theoretically were lower under
Aer1 due to less oxygen supply, the moisture and heat losses under Aer1
simultaneously were lower. Therefore, the actual temperatures under
Aer1 were higher than those under Aer3 apart from upper-layer tem-
peratures because the temperature rise synthetically reflected the pro-
duction and loss of heat and moisture in the aerobic pretreatment
process.

In addition, an entirely decreased trend was observed in the C/N
ratios except for the slight increase under Aer1R3T3 and Aer3R1T3 at 84
and 96 h, respectively [Fig. 3 (d)], possibly because of higher nitrogen
retention than nitrogen degradation. In the first 84 h, the C/N ratios
under Aer2R1T2, Aer3R2T1, and Aer3R3T2 descended the fastest. At the
end of aerobic pretreatment for 120 h, the maximal C/N ratio decrease
was obtained under Aer2R2T3, followed by Aer3R1T3, and the minimal
descent occurred under Aer1R3T3. All the final C/N ratios ranged from
26.40 to 29.21 after aerobic pretreatment. Under the same initial C/N
ratio of 30 and oxygen concentration range of 13%–17%, the final C/N
ratios (26.43 and 26.40) of Aer2R1T2 and Aer2R2T3 were almost equal to
that (26.40) of CN2R2, which indicated that the higher temperature rise
obtained under Aer2R1T2 contributed to the reduction of the C/N ratio
and a low aeration rate was favorable. In conclusion, the final C/N ratios
of the feedstocks undergoing aerobic pretreatment under dynamic
aeration could meet the C/N ratios required for the following co-AD.
The pH values increased in the first 24 h except for Aer3R1T3 and
Aer3R3T2 [Fig. 3 (e)]. Although most reports elucidated that the pH
value slightly decreased in the early stage of aerobic treatment because
microorganisms rapidly utilized the dissolved OM to produce small
molecular organic acids, some studies also found that the pH value
might be unvaried or slightly elevated because the feedstocks, for
example, manure, biogas residue, etc. or the weak alkaline ammonia
generated during ammoniation process of organic nitrogen acted as a
buffer (Rodrigues et al., 2021). Furthermore, Beck-Friis et al. (2001)
found that the temperature shift from the mesophilic phase to the
thermophilic phase occurred in parallel with the pH shift from acidic to
alkaline in the initial stage of aerobic treatment and bacteria with a high
rate of organic decomposition under alkaline circumstances proliferated
as pH increased, speeding up the elimination of OM. Therefore, the pH
values showed different trends of increasing and then decreasing, or
decreasing and then increasing after 24 h with the mineralization and
utilization of organic acids by microorganisms, nitrification and con-
version of ammonium nitrogen into nitrate nitrogen, volatilization of
free ammonia during aeration, and continuous decomposition of OM
and organic nitrogen (Zhu et al., 2021), reflecting the dynamic equi-
librium of VFAs from OM decomposition and ammonia from organic
nitrogen ammonification. The pH values ranged from 7.71 to 8.98
during the aerobic pretreatment in this study, which was similar to the
optimal pretreatment range of pH (7.96–8.80) obtained by Chen et al.
(2013) for VFAs production during the AD of waste-activated sludge and
food waste.
The removals of lignocellulose containing cellulose, hemicellulose,
and lignin increased as the pretreatment duration increased, as shown in
Fig. 3 (f). The lignocellulose elimination efficiencies under Aer1 were
relatively lower than those under Aer2 and Aer3. Although the pre-
treatment time of 120 h under Aer3R1T3 was longer than that under
Aer3R3T2 (84 h), the lignocellulose removals of Aer3R1T3 were not su-
perior to those of Aer3R3T2. Furthermore, the hemicellulose removal
rates (5.54%–8.83%) were higher than those of cellulose (2.76%–
5.74%) and lignin (0.61%–1.30%) because hemicellulose was a het-
erogeneous polymer composed of monosaccharides including xylose,
arabinose, and galactose, and was more unstable than those of the cel-
lulose with macromolecular polysaccharides and the lignin with phe-
nylpropanoid. Lignin removals obtained under Aer2R1T2, Aer3R2T1, and
Aer3R3T2 only reached 1.05%, 1.20%, and 1.30%, respectively, and
were similar to the lignin removal of 1.18% obtained under CN2R3,
which further elucidated that the lignin removal capacity of aerobic
pretreatment at high solids loading was low. In addition, the oxygen
concentration, aeration rate, and aerobic pretreatment time interac-
tively affected the cumulative aeration time, which determined the
energy consumption and pretreatment effect of aeration operation
during aerobic pretreatment. The accumulative aeration time of 59 min
obtained under Aer3R1T3 was the longest. The aeration durations were
similar for Aer2R1T2 and Aer3R2T1 (20 and 22 min) but did not exceed
12 min under other pretreatment conditions.
3.3. Effects of aerobic pretreatment under dynamic aeration on co-
anaerobic digestion characteristics of corn stover and swine manure
3.3.1. Methanogenesis
As shown in Fig. 4, the accumulative methane production of the
control only reached 4.37 L, which corroborated that the dry co-AD of
corn stover and swine manure without pretreatment could not run
smoothly. The daily methane production of Aer2R1T2 increased rapidly
on the second day, reached the maximal peak value on the fifth day, then
slightly fluctuated up and down within 6–8 d, and peaked again on the
eleventh day after a significant fall because of acidification. Aer2R2T3
showed two peak values at 12 d and 16–19 d, respectively. Relatively
low peaks occurred between 11 and 17 d, respectively, for Aer2R3T1,
Aer3R1T3, and Aer3R2T1. Although Aer1R1T1 and Aer3R3T2 reached their
peaks earlier in the first five days, their peak values were lower than
Aer2R1T2. Therefore, Aer2R1T2 outperformed other samples, and its total
cumulative and VS methane production for 25 days reached 338.76 L
and 258.93 L/kg VS, followed by Aer2R2T3 with 255.97 L and 234.86 L/
kg VS. Two similar cumulative and VS methane yields (122.72 and
134.34 L and 201.50 and 196.83 L/kg VS) were for Aer2R3T1 and
Aer3R1T3. Approximate yields also occurred for Aer3R2T1 and Aer3R3T2
(101.80 and 107.87 L and 142.99 and 155.66 L/kg VS). The methane
yields under Aer1 were not up to par and only reached 63.84, 33.66, and
42.71 L and 90.21, 60.04, and 81.68 L/kg VS, respectively, for Aer1R1T1,
Aer1R2T2, and Aer1R3T3. Therefore, the aerobic pretreatment under
dynamic aeration based on the oxygen concentration range of 13%–17%
promoted the rapid start-up of co-AD and increased methane production
of corn stover and swine manure, and a lower aeration rate and a
moderate pretreatment time were more favorable for the subsequent co-
AD. Although aerobic pretreatment with high solids loading had the
potential to partially destroy the crystalline structure of lignocellulose
and hydrolyze some macromolecular OM into tiny molecules of organic
acids that microorganisms could use, microorganisms simultaneously
devoured some OM for their metabolism and reproduction, particularly
the soluble OM in swine manure, thereby the overall OM amount was
decreased for co-AD. Therefore, excessive pretreatment time was not
advisable.
3.3.2. PH, ammonia nitrogen, and volatile fatty acids
The variations in pH characterize a synergistic effect of the solvation
equilibrium of CO2 and H2S between the vapor and liquid phases, the
acid-base balance in the liquid phase, and the ion dissolution equilib-
rium between the solid and liquid phases (Wang et al., 2020). As shown
in Fig. 5 (a), The initial pH values of pretreated corn stover and swine
manure ranged from 6.71 to 7.35 at the beginning of co-AD and the pH
values showed significant downward and then upward fluctuations in
the first nineteen days of co-AD, indicating that self-buffering system of
CO3
2−/HCO3
−and NH4
+/NH3⋅H2O had not yet formed (Mao et al., 2017).
The pH values gradually stabilized after 19 d and reached 6.82–7.26 by
the end of co-AD as acidification and methanation approached equilib-
rium apart from the control. In comparison, the pH value of the control
fluctuated between 5.31 and 5.73 until the end of co-AD after a sharp
decline in the first ten days, which further elucidated that excessive
VFAs inhibited the initiation of co-AD.
Although ammonia nitrogen is integral for anaerobic microbial
synthesis, excess free ammonia transformed from organic nitrogen
might harm microorganisms in the ammonium/ammonia balance due to
its easy cell membrane crossing (Ruiz-S´anchez et al., 2018). All the
ammonia nitrogen contents varied between 50 and 358 mg/L during
co-AD, as shown in Fig. 5 (b), which was less than the ammonia nitrogen

system, the ammonia nitrogen usually first shows an increasing trend
until the ammonium nitrogen consumed by hydrolytic and methano-
genic bacteria and the free ammonia lost through evaporation exceed
the ammonia nitrogen amount produced from the decomposition of
proteins and amino acids, and then begins to decrease and ammonia
nitrogen and VFAs maintained a dynamic equilibrium (Rubeˇzius et al.,
2020). However, the ammonia nitrogen contents of the control in this
study continuously increased during co-AD. The ammonia nitrogen
contents were the highest under Aer3, followed by Aer2, and the
ammonia nitrogen contents were the lowest under Aer1. Amino acid
oxidizing enzymes converted more amino acids into ammonia nitrogen
under Aer3 due to an adequate oxygen supply (Rubeˇzius et al., 2020),
thereby maintaining lower C/N ratios and higher ammonia nitrogen
contents at the onset of co-AD and even during co-AD. In comparison,
the ammonification reactions of Aer1 were not active during co-AD
because of poor pretreatment effect and relatively high C/N ratio.
Therefore, the ammonia nitrogen levels fluctuated less under Aer1.
Methanogens need to decompose VFAs to generate methane, and
VFAs are critical intermediates in the AD process (Chu et al., 2021). As
shown in Fig. 5 (c), the initial VFA contents (2.63–4.95 g/L) of pre-
treated corn stover and swine manure were higher than that of the
control, which further elucidated that aerobic pretreatment could
accumulate a certain amount of VFAs and active hydrolytic acidification
microorganisms for the subsequent co-AD, thereby accelerating the
start-up of co-AD (Saritpongteeraka et al., 2015). The variations in VFA
contents followed the typical pattern that first climbed quickly, then
declined, and finally tended to stabilize. The VFA peaks under Aer2 were
relatively high. Aer2R1T2 peaked on the fourth day, while the maximal
peak value was under Aer2R2T3 on the seventh day. The VFA content of
the control showed a significant increase in the first four days before
becoming essentially constant, which matched its variations in methane
production and pH value and further defined that irreparable rancidity
occurred. Although the pH value and the ammonia nitrogen and VFA
contents of Aer1R2T2 and Aer1R3T3 did not show inhibition, the methane
produced was less throughout co-AD. Therefore, a pseudo-steady state
might be exhibited under Aer1 due to the interactions between pH,
ammonia nitrogen, and VFAs, characterizing stable operation but low
methane production (Lü et al., 2013). In addition, the VFAs mainly
included acetic, propionic, and butyric acids. Acetic acid and propionic
acid showed similar fluctuations to the overall VFA level and peaked at
3.72–6.45 g/L and 3.04–4.10 g/L at 4, 7, and 13 d, respectively. Xu et al.
(2020) reported that approximately 70% of the methane came from
acetic acid during AD. Rubeˇzius et al. (2020) found that aerobic pre-
treatment promoted the acetate acid conversion from VFAs in the AD
process of poultry manure, while acetic acid did not constitute a high
portion of the total VFAs after ten days in this study because of the
microbial predilection utilization for acetic acid. The propionic acid
level at the start of co-AD exceeded the inhibitory threshold of 900 mg/L
(Wang et al., 2009) due to the presence of corn stover in the feedstocks.
Yu et al. (2018) reported that the more corn stover added, the more
propionic acid accumulated during AD. However, propionic acid did not
appreciably impede methane production in this study since it could be
oxidized into acetic acid when the acetic acid content gradually fell and
consumed by methanobacteria (Wang et al., 2022a),.
In conclusion, a moderate oxygen concentration range of 13%–17%
(Aer2) and a lower aeration rate of 0.1 m3/(min⋅m3) (R1) were prefer-
able for the aerobic pretreatment of corn stover and swine manure with
high solids loading. Aer2R1T2 was optimum for temperature rise and
methane production but reached its maximal temperature at 72 h
instead of the 84 h corresponding to T2. Furthermore, the aeration time
would extend to achieve the target oxygen concentration at a reduced
aeration rate. Meanwhile, aeration time increased with the duration of
aerobic pretreatment. Therefore, the pretreatment duration was further
studied in the following study to examine the feasibility of a 72-h pre-
treatment duration.
3.4. Effects of pretreatment duration, inoculum loading, daily leachate
reflux repetitions, and inoculation layers on methane production of
aerobic-pretreated corn stover and swine manure
The effects of pretreatment durations (72, 84, and 96 h for A1, A2,
and A3), inoculum loading (20%, 30%, and 40% for B1, B2, and B3), daily
leachate reflux repetitions (once, twice, and thrice for C1, C2, and C3),
and inoculation layers (single-layer, double-layer, and triple-layer for
D1, D2, and D3) on methane production and VFAs variations are as
shown in Fig. 6.
As shown in Fig. 6 (a), although the accumulative methane yield of
A2 was somewhat less than that of Aer2R1T2 under the same 84-h pre-
treatment, the daily and accumulative methane production under A2
was superior to those under A1 and A3. A prolonged pretreatment period
of 96 h under A3 was not favorable. The daily methane production of A2
peaked in the first five days and was earlier than A1 and A3. The cu-
mulative methane yields A1, A2, and A3 were 292.64, 308.05, and
258.16 L, respectively, and their methane contents were 36.98%–
42.81% in biogas. The VS methane yields of A1, A2, and A3 reached
229.95, 247.79, and 205.58 L/kg VS, respectively, and the maximum at
84 h was slightly lower than that (258.93 L/kg VS) under Aer2R1T2. In
addition, increasing the oxygen concentration and aeration rate might
increase the power consumption and instead exacerbate the harmful
impact of cold air on pretreatment and was not advisable. Therefore, the
optimal oxygen concentration range, aeration rate, pretreatment dura-
tion of 13%–17% (Aer2), 0.1 m3/(min⋅m3) (R1), and 84 h (A2) were used
for the following trials to further improve methane production in terms
of inoculation method and leachate reflux.
As shown in Fig. 6 (b), the daily and cumulative methane production
of B1, B2, and B3 represented a rising tendency with an increase in
inoculum loading and peaked within the first five days. The cumulative
and VS methane outputs reached 227.73, 343.40, and 444.58 L and
190.25, 249.68, and 266.30 L/kg VS, respectively, for B1, B2, and B3, and
the optimal B3 with inoculum loading of 40% was superior to Aer2R1T2
and A2 with inoculum loading of 30%. The average methane contents in
biogas reached 44.94% for B3 and were increased by 6.93% and 3.24%
compared to B1 and B2. Therefore, the inoculum loading was crucial for
the pretreated corn stover and swine manure to enter co-AD rapidly and
generate methane efficiently because the inoculum riched in hydrolytic
acidification and methanogenic microorganisms (Yue et al., 2023).
As shown in Fig. 6 (c), the daily methane production of C1, C2, and C3
peaked in the first five days. The cumulative and VS methane yields
reached 271.40, 337.02, and 404.42 L and 219.33, 234.74, and 260.14
L/kg VS, respectively, for C1, C2, and C3, and the leachate reflux
repeated three times per day was optimum. Meanwhile, the methane
contents of C3 increased by 4.37%–7.91% compared to C1 and C2.
Multiple leachate backflows were beneficial for promoting methane
production in the dry co-AD process because the leachate with higher
moisture content could not only dilute the inhibitory compounds
affecting AD and enhance the heat and mass transfer characteristics of
the feedstocks but also improve the opportunities for microorganisms to
contact with the substrates and promote the degradation of organic
compounds (Song et al., 2023). Although methane bacteria are sensitive
to leachate flushing because the methanogenic bacteria typically require
a longer time of 10–15 d to reproduce compared to the 24–36 h and
80–90 h of the hydrolysis and acidification microorganisms (Deublein
and Steinhauser, 2008), the leachate reflux of thrice was still favorable
in this study. In addition, the methane yield of C2 was lower than that of
B3 at the same inoculum loading of 40% and daily leachate reflux rep-
etitions of twice, and the methane production of C3 still did not exceed
that of B3 even when leachate reflux was increased to thrice every day.

In conclusion, the inoculum loading, leachate reflux repetitions, and
stratified inoculation were critical to ensuring the well-functioning co-
AD of aerobic-pretreated corn stover and swine manure. Although the
decrease in ambient temperature diminished methane production, the
methane yields achieved under the optimal conditions of inoculum
loading of 40%, daily leachate reflux repetitions of thrice, and double-

namic aeration was favorable for dry co-AD of corn stover and swine
manure, and integrated aerobic-anaerobic digestion was a competitive
approach for the low-cost operation of dry AD at different scales.
4. Conclusions
Integrated aerobic-anaerobic digestion of highly solids-loaded corn
stover and swine manure was viable. Dynamic aeration accelerated the
temperature rise of aerobic pretreatment and enhanced the methano-
genic performance during the dry co-AD of corn stover and swine
manure. Inoculum addition and leachate reflux were critical for the dry
co-AD process to operate steadily apart from aerobic pretreatment. The
optimized regulation of dynamic aeration, inoculum addition, and
leachate reflux improved the integrated aerobic-anaerobic digestion
system’s ability to resist low temperatures to some extent and the
inoculum loading was more correlated with increasing methane pro-
duction than leachate reflux repetitions and stratified inoculation. The
optimal conditions obtained in this study were an oxygen concentration
range of 13%–17%, an aeration rate of 0.10 m3/(min⋅m3), a pretreat-
ment time of 84 h, and an inoculation loading of 40%, refluxing thrice
per day, and double-layer inoculation. The maximal cumulative and VS
methane yields reached 444.58 L and 266.30 L/kg VS, respectively.
